title: "Directing the Quality Analyst"
order: 27
---

## The finish line

By the end of this course you can take a deviation write-up, a CAPA (corrective and
preventive action), a validation package, or a vendor risk assessment your Quality Analyst
(QA) wrote, and read it the way an FDA investigator or AABB assessor will: cold, a year from
now, with her not in the room. You'll catch the gaps they'd catch before the document leaves
your desk. You'll also know which events have to reach you directly, which ones go past you,
and how fast.

You already review a direct report's work every week: change tickets, postmortems, runbooks,
a vendor's security questionnaire. None of that changes. What changes is who reads the
document after you, and what they're allowed to do about a gap. This course is about the
difference between "I'd approve this in IT" and "this would survive an inspector."

## Before you start

This course builds on everything published so far:

- [Reading a CFR citation](../../foundations/reading-a-cfr-citation/index.qmd)
- [Regulatory landscape orientation](../../foundations/regulatory-landscape-orientation/index.qmd)
  — you'll check that your QA labels regulation, guidance, AABB Standard, and industry
  practice correctly in everything she writes.
- [Risk and controls vocabulary](../../foundations/risk-and-controls-vocabulary/index.qmd)
  — likelihood, severity, detectability, and correction versus corrective action are the
  words you'll use to push back.
- [Blood Center Operations](../blood-center-operations/index.qmd), especially
  [BECS in the pipeline](../blood-center-operations/becs-in-the-pipeline/index.qmd), whose
  patch fight and validation impact assessment come back in module 4.
- [Quality System Essentials](../quality-system-essentials/index.qmd), the whole course.
  It taught what a good deviation, CAPA, change, and management-review packet look like.
  This course teaches you to find what's missing from a real one.

## The six modules

Each module is one sitting, and each has its own finish line.

1. **What your QA produces, and who owns it.** Name what your QA produces, who writes,
   approves, and only needs to see each piece, and what your own signature means on it.
   Learn one short test for reviewing any of it.
2. **Reviewing deviation and CAPA write-ups.** Read a real (and flawed) write-up the way an
   assessor would. Find the missing reasoning, the evidence that doesn't prove the claim,
   the scope that stops too soon, and the effectiveness check that can't fail. Then send it
   back so the second draft is better.
3. **Escalation: what has to reach you, and how fast.** Sort any event into "call me now,"
   "tell me today," or "your call, tell me at our one-on-one." Know which events go past
   you, and which ones your QA must be able to take around you. Write escalation criteria
   that beat the regulatory clocks instead of chasing them.
4. **Reviewing a validation package: the decision trail.** Review a BECS (Blood
   Establishment Computer Software) validation impact assessment or test summary for scope,
   criteria set before testing, failures handled honestly, and sign-offs in the right order.
5. **Reviewing a vendor risk assessment: the decision trail.** Check whether your QA's
   evidence actually covers the service Lakeshore buys and the risk that triggered the
   review, and whether someone with authority owns the risk decision.
6. **Coaching your QA and reporting upward.** Turn repeated review findings into coaching
   that changes how she works, and give her more decision rights as her judgment proves out.
   Report quality, IT, and risk performance to your CIO with measures that don't reward
   hiding problems.

## How deep each module goes, and why

Modules 1, 2, 3, and 6 go to full depth now. Everything they need is already built: the
quality system machinery, the regulatory clocks, and the risk vocabulary.

Modules 4 and 5 are deliberately narrower for now, and you should know that going in. The
courses that teach validation methodology (`csv-and-becs`) and vendor and third-party risk
(`vendor-and-third-party-risk-management`) aren't built yet. So these two modules teach
the half of the review you can do today. That half is the **decision trail**: what was
decided, on what evidence, against what criteria, by whom, and in what order. An assessor
asks those questions first, and you can answer them without being a validation engineer or
a SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) reader. What these modules won't do yet is
teach you whether the testing was technically enough or what a SOC 2 report's fine print
means. Each one says plainly where that line is. Both will be deepened once those courses
exist.

Modules appear in the sidebar as they're built.
